I read about two thousand files a year, and on the first pass I give each one roughly seven minutes. People are shocked by that number, and they should not be. Seven minutes is enough, because after the first hundred you know exactly where the information is. What I want to say to a room full of counsellors is this. The files I remember are not the ones with the longest lists. Every file has a list. The files I remember tell me what has changed about the person, and that is a different sentence with a different tense in it. I went to Canada and I played in a league is a fact. I have not needed a translation since March is a person. And please, all of you, talk to your students about the word significant. They write that a experience was significant and they stop there, as if the adjective did the work. It does not. Show me what came after it. I can judge a consequence. I cannot judge an adjective, and after two thousand files I do not even read them any more.

The thing nobody tells you about the first month is that it is very easy to waste it. I wasted mine. There were four other Brazilians in my building and we did everything together, and it was comfortable, and my English did not move a centimetre in thirty days. What fixed it was not a course. I joined a student club where nobody spoke Portuguese, and I went twice a week even on the days I did not want to go. Since then a lot has changed, and the one I notice most is that I have stopped building sentences in my head before I open my mouth. I answer while I am still thinking, which sounds like a small thing and is not. About the certificate, because everybody asks me. I took mine before I applied and it opened the door, so I am not going to pretend it does not matter. But I tell people the same thing every time. The certificate proves the level, it does not build it, and those two things have to happen in that order or you just pay twice.
